```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE)
```

This vignette states, for every model of mortensor, the model equation,
the estimation method, how the forecast is generated, the defaults, and
which sources of uncertainty the forecast draws contain. It is meant as
the basis of a methods section. `summary()` of a fitted model prints the
same information for the actual fit, `mt_parameters()` returns the
estimates.

```{r}
library(mortensor)
x <- mt_example(deaths = "single", years = 1995:2019)
summary(mt_fit(lee_carter(), x))
```

Notation: `m(x,t,i)` is the central death rate at age `x` in year `t` in
stratum `i` (deaths divided by exposure), `D` deaths, `E` exposures.

## Data steps that affect every model

| Step | What mortensor does | Function |
|---|---|---|
| Exposures | mid-year population, or the mean of the populations at the start and the end of the year (1 January or 31 December counts; Preston, Heuveline and Guillot 2001) | `mt_as_exposure(type = )` |
| Suppressed cells | raking (iterative proportional fitting; Deming and Stephan 1940) of the missing counts to published totals, within optional bounds; cells that no published total covers get the mean of a Poisson distribution truncated to the bounds | `mt_fill_suppressed()` |
| Unknown ages | distributed over the age groups of the same stratum and year in proportion to the known deaths | `mt_data()` |
| Ungrouping | penalised composite link model with exposures (Rizzi, Gampe and Eilers 2015), its fitted values without rescaling to the group totals (`preserve_totals = FALSE`), or monotone interpolation of cumulative counts (`method = "monotone"`; Hyman 1983); the exposure of an open interval of the grid (for example 100+) is split over single years up to `omega` by the PCLM of the exposures (`open_split = "pclm"`, default, as Rizzi, Gampe and Eilers 2015) or with stationary-population weights (`"stationary"`, package-specific) | `mt_ungroup()`, `step_ungroup()` |
| Smoothing | over age (Poisson P-splines; Whittaker; GAM), over time (Whittaker) or the age-period surface (P-splines, Currie, Durban and Eilers 2004; quasi-Poisson `te(age, year)` GAM, Wood 2017); age 0 is not smoothed; models are fitted to the smoothed rates, their residuals and backtest scales come from the raw rates, and their predictive draws add Poisson deaths to the forecast rates (also for models of observed rates); smoothing over time narrows the intervals of models with a period index (check coverage, `recalibrated()`) | `mt_smooth()`, `step_smooth()`, `mt_smooth_check()` |
| Zero deaths | models on log rates use 0.5 deaths in a cell without deaths | |

All preprocessing steps given as `prep` are refitted on every training
window of a backtest.

## Single-population models

### Lee-Carter: `lee_carter()`

`log m(x,t) = a(x) + b(x) k(t)`, with `sum b(x) = 1` and `sum k(t) = 0`
(Lee and Carter 1992).

* **Estimation**: Poisson maximum likelihood (default; Brouhns, Denuit
  and Vermunt 2002) or SVD of the log rates (`method = "svd"`, as
  `demography::lca()`), with `k(t)` re-estimated to match the observed
  total deaths (`adjust = "dt"`), the deaths by age (`"dxt"`, Booth,
  Maindonald and Smith 2002) or life expectancy (`"e0"`, Lee and Miller
  2001). `choose_period = TRUE` fits the model to the longest recent period
  over which `k(t)` was close to linear (Booth, Maindonald and Smith 2002).
  Age groups without any death get a constant rate of 0.5 deaths over the
  training period and `b(x) = 0`. When the Poisson likelihood has no
  finite maximum (very sparse counts), `b(x)` is shrunk towards equal
  shares by a ridge penalty, and if that fails too the SVD estimates are
  used. These are safeguards of this package and are reported as
  warnings.
* **Forecast**: `k(t)` follows a random walk with drift; the drift and
  the innovation variance are estimated from the year-to-year changes of
  `k(t)`.
* **Jump-off**: fitted rates of the last year (default) or observed rates
  (`jump_off = "observed"`; Lee and Miller 2001).
* **Uncertainty in the draws**: innovations of `k(t)` and the uncertainty
  of its drift. `a(x)` and `b(x)` are fixed; `bootstrap = TRUE` (Poisson
  resamples of the fitted deaths; Renshaw and Haberman 2008) or
  `bootstrapped()` adds their uncertainty. Predictive draws add Poisson
  variation of the deaths given the rates, the observation model of the
  Poisson Lee-Carter model (Brouhns, Denuit and Vermunt 2002).
* **Negative binomial deaths** (`family = "nb"`, opt-in; Delwarde, Denuit
  and Partrat 2007): the deaths are negative binomial with variance
  `mu + phi mu^2` and one dispersion parameter `phi` for all cells. `a`,
  `b`, `k` and `phi` are estimated by maximum likelihood with the paper's
  Newton updates of one parameter set at a time; `k(t)` follows a random
  walk with drift. Predictive draws add negative binomial variation with
  the estimated `phi`. Package-specific: the updates start from the
  Poisson estimates, `phi` is found by Newton steps on its logarithm and is
  0 when the data show no overdispersion, the constraints are `sum b = 1`
  and `sum k = 0` (the paper states none), and the draws contain the drift
  uncertainty (the paper gives point forecasts). Not available with
  `method = "svd"` or `choose_period = TRUE`. On French men and women
  (ages 0-99, 1950-2002, data of the demography package) the estimates of
  `phi` and of the drift agree with those of the paper within 1%. In an
  example backtest on England & Wales men aged 55-89 (origins 1996-2001,
  10 years ahead), the CRPS of log rates was 0.072 with both families and
  the 95% intervals covered 0.67 of the observed rates (Poisson 0.63).
* **Rotation** (`rotate = TRUE`; Li, Lee and Gerland 2013): as life
  expectancy at birth rises from `e0_start` (80) to `e0_end` (102), the age
  pattern of decline moves from `b(x)` to an ultimate pattern with equal
  decline below 65 (the mean of `b` over ages 15-64) and the shape of
  `b(x)` above. The weight follows a sine curve with `power` 0.5. In each
  path and year the index is solved again so that life expectancy at birth
  stays that of the unrotated forecast; rotation therefore changes the age
  pattern of the forecast only. The defaults are those of the paper. The
  paper takes the weights from the life expectancy of both sexes combined
  and illustrates the method with the median path; here each stratum and
  each draw is rotated with its own path of life expectancy. In MortCast
  (Sevcikova et al. 2016) the path of life expectancy comes from a
  separate model; here it is that of the Lee-Carter draws. Rotation needs
  ages from 0 and computes life tables for every path and year, which is
  about 20 times slower.

### Compositional data model: `coda()`

`clr(d(x,t) / a(x)) = b(x) k(t)`, the Lee-Carter model in compositional
form (Oeppen 2008) as published by Bergeron-Boucher et al. (2017), where
`d(x,t)` are the life-table deaths (radix 1), `a(x)` their geometric mean
over the years, closed to 1, and `clr` the centred log-ratio
transformation. The model forecasts the distribution of deaths by age, so
the forecast deaths always form a life table. The unit tests reproduce
the estimates and point forecasts of the authors' code (CoDaForecast.R,
supplementary material of the paper) on French data, for one population
and for the coherent model.

* **Estimation**: first component of the SVD of the centred log-ratios;
  `b` and `k` sum to zero, with signs that make `k(t)` increase. Zero
  deaths are replaced multiplicatively in each year (Appendix C of the
  paper).
* **Old ages**: with single-year age groups from 80 to at least 89
  (`open = "auto"`, default), the rates from age 80 are replaced in every
  year by a Kannisto model (Thatcher, Kannisto and Vaupel 1998) fitted by
  Poisson maximum likelihood to ages 80-100 and extended to age 120, where
  the life table closes. Other age groups do not allow this extension: the
  deaths of the open interval are the survivors at its lower bound, and
  its log death rate is regressed on the indexes (`open = "regression"`,
  package-specific).
* **Forecast**: `k(t)` follows an ARIMA(0,1,1) model with drift, fitted by
  maximum likelihood (`order`, `drift`). Its point forecast is shifted so
  that the first step equals the drift (eq. 20 of the paper), which
  removes the break that the moving-average term causes in the first
  forecast year. Deaths are transformed back to rates through the life
  table. `order = c(0, 1, 0)` gives the random walk with drift of Lee and
  Carter (1992), the default of the R package MortalityForecast
  (Pascariu).
* **Jump-off**: observed deaths of the last year, changed by the model
  (default; Appendix G of the paper), or fitted deaths
  (`jump_off = "fitted"`). Appendix G also mentions smoothing the last
  year with P-splines for Poisson counts (Camarda 2012), next to the
  jump-off of the Lee-Carter models; the authors' code starts the CoDa
  forecasts from the deaths of the last year with the Kannisto rates from
  age 80, and so does the package.
* **Coherent version** (`coherent = TRUE` or `common_by`):
  `clr(d(x,t,i) / a(x,i)) = B(x) K(t) + b(x,i) k(t,i)`. The common
  component is the model above fitted to the arithmetic mean of the death
  rates of the strata of a group. `K(t)` follows the index model, each
  `k(t,i)` an ARIMA(1,1,0) model without drift (`order_dev`,
  `drift_dev`), whose point forecast levels off: the point forecasts of
  the strata do not diverge, and their intervals still widen with the
  horizon. `order_dev = c(1, 0, 0)` gives AR(1) deviations with a mean
  (Li and Lee 2005), which stay bounded in distribution.
* **Uncertainty**: the bootstrap of Appendix B of the paper. The residuals
  of the clr fit are resampled cell by cell, `b` and `k` are estimated
  again (`a` is kept), the ARIMA model is refitted, and index paths are
  simulated with resampled innovations; `ceiling(sqrt(n_draws))` refits
  share the draws (the paper: 100 refits with 100 paths each). In the
  coherent model the common and the stratum components are simulated
  independently. The draws are centred on the point forecast part by
  part, as in the authors' code (the paper shifts the bounds of the
  intervals of life expectancy). Predictive draws add Poisson variation of
  the deaths given the rates. All ages have equal weight on the clr
  scale, so the noise of ages with few deaths enters `k(t)`: intervals can
  be wider than those of Lee-Carter. In an example backtest on England &
  Wales men (ages 30-100, origins 1996-2001, 10 years ahead) the 95%
  intervals covered 0.97 of the observed rates at horizons 1-4 and 0.71
  at horizon 10: the moving-average coefficient of the index was at -1,
  so the index paths added little uncertainty beyond that of the drift.
* **Deviations**: life tables with `a_x = n / 2` at age 0 (the authors'
  code: 0.06); the number of refits; the centring of the draws and the
  regression of the open interval described above. Zero deaths follow the
  formula of Appendix C; the authors' code closes the composition after
  the imputation, so that a zero gets `delta / (1 + z delta)` there.
* **Related methods not implemented**: more components with functional
  time series models of their scores (Shang and Haberman 2020) and the
  alpha-transformation in place of the clr, which handles zero counts
  (Shang and Haberman 2025; Dong et al. 2025 for causes of death).

### Random walk with drift: `rwd()`

Each age: `log m(x,t) = log m(x,t-1) + mu(x) + e(x,t)`.

* **Estimation**: drift as the mean year-to-year change (over the last
  `drift_window` years); innovations are resampled vectors of observed
  changes across ages (`innovations = "bootstrap"`, keeps the correlation
  between ages) or normal (`"gaussian"`).
* **Uncertainty**: innovations and drift. The observed changes contain the
  Poisson noise of two years, so the intervals are wide where deaths are
  few, and over long horizons very wide. The draws describe observed
  rates, so predictive draws add nothing.

The random walk with drift observed with noise (local level model with
drift; Harvey 1989) is `arima_series(order = c(0, 1, 1), drift = TRUE)`,
its reduced form, below. `rwd(observation_noise = TRUE)`, a moment
estimator of this package for the same model, is deprecated.

### Two-dimensional P-splines: `p_splines()`

The deaths are Poisson, and the log death rates are a smooth surface
over age and year: a tensor product of B-splines whose neighbouring
coefficients are penalised by differences of order `pord` (default 2)
over age and over years (Currie, Durban and Eilers 2004). The code
follows `Mort2Dsmooth()` and `predict.Mort2Dsmooth()` of the R package
MortalitySmooth 2.3.4 (Camarda 2015) and reproduces their fitted values,
forecasts and standard errors for given smoothing parameters.

* **Estimation**: penalised Poisson likelihood; the two smoothing
  parameters minimise the BIC (default) or the AIC. Cells with missing
  deaths or exposures get weight 0, so the surface interpolates them.
  `overdispersion = TRUE` takes a dispersion parameter into the choice of
  the smoothing parameters and into the draws. `infant = TRUE` gives the
  first year of life coefficients of its own (Camarda 2019).
* **Forecast**: part of the fit. The basis over years is extended over the
  forecast years, which enter with weight 0; their coefficients follow
  from the penalty. With `pord = 2` each age continues the trend of its
  last years about linearly on the log scale.
* **Uncertainty**: draws from the normal approximation of the
  coefficients, with the covariance of the penalised likelihood. Over the
  forecast years the penalty acts as a prior: the variance grows with the
  horizon, the faster the smaller the smoothing parameter over years.
  Draws are paths of the whole surface, correlated over ages and years.
  Predictive draws add Poisson variation of the deaths given the rates.
* **Package-specific**: knots about five years apart also for age groups
  (counted in the single years that the cells span), and the search of
  the smoothing parameters (a grid with steps of 1 on the log10 scale,
  then a continuous search; MortalitySmooth uses two grids).
* **Use**: each age continues the trend of its last years. In example
  backtests (10 years ahead from six origins), the CRPS of log rates was
  0.035 against 0.071 for Lee-Carter on England & Wales men aged 30-100,
  and 0.115 against 0.085 on French women aged 0-100, where the surface
  extrapolated local trends at ages 65 and over. On England & Wales men
  the 95% intervals of life
  expectancy at 30 covered 0.40 of the observed values (Lee-Carter 0.90):
  the intervals of summary measures are narrow.

### Constrained P-splines: `cp_splines()`

The CP-spline model of Camarda (2019) is the model of `p_splines()` with
coefficients of their own for the first year of life, whose forecast is
held to the age pattern and the time trends of the data years. The code
is written from the paper; the author's code was used to check results.

* **Constraints**: in every data year, the derivatives of the fitted log
  rates over age (rate of ageing) and over years (rate of change) are
  computed. Their central 95% range (`level_ageing`) and central 50% range
  (`level_change`) over the data years bound the forecast at each age.
  Asymmetric penalties with weight `kappa` (1e4) pull forecast
  derivatives outside the bounds back towards them, so forecast age
  patterns keep the shape of the fitted ones, and the change of each age
  stays within the range of its past change.
* **Uncertainty**: residual bootstrap (section 3.2.2 of the paper). The
  deviance residuals of the fit are resampled and turned into bootstrap
  deaths, and the constrained forecast is computed again for each of
  `n_boot` samples (100 by default; the paper uses 1000). The draws carry
  the uncertainty of the fit only: the forecast has no innovations, and
  Camarda (2019) notes that the intervals are often narrower than those
  of other methods. Predictive draws add Poisson variation of the deaths.
* **Package-specific**: the choices of `p_splines()`, the rate of ageing
  at age 0 for age groups, and the bootstrap deaths of cells without
  deaths.
* **Use**: the model needs at least 10 data years, and the first year of
  life as its own age group for the infant coefficients. In the same
  example backtests, the CRPS of log rates was 0.066 against 0.085
  for Lee-Carter on French women, and the CRPS of life expectancy at birth
  0.122 against 0.239. On England & Wales men the rates of change of
  1961-2001 held back the faster decline after 2001 (CRPS 0.058, against
  0.071 for Lee-Carter and 0.035 for `p_splines()`). The 95% intervals
  covered 0.53 (England & Wales) and 0.62 (France) of the observed
  rates.

### Rates of mortality improvement: `bohk_rau()`

Bohk-Ewald and Rau (2017) forecast rates of mortality improvement
`rho(x,t) = 1 - m(x,t+1) / m(x,t)` of death rates smoothed with
two-dimensional P-splines. A Bayesian core model describes the
improvements of every age over the years of the base period: an
exponential curve `exp(b1(x) + b2(x) log t)` (`core = "exponential"`,
default), under which improvements can level off and increases of
mortality cannot be forecast, or a linear trend `b1(x) + b2(x) t`
(`"linear"`). Hierarchical priors tie the curves of the ages together.
The trends differ between ages, so the age pattern of decline changes
over the forecast.

* **Estimation**: MCMC with the settings of the paper (five chains of
  5,200 iterations, the first 200 discarded, every fifth kept). The
  sampler is written for this package (the paper uses JAGS);
  `mt_parameters()` reports Gelman-Rubin statistics, and values above 1.1
  give a warning. A fit takes about 6 seconds per stratum for 71 ages and
  36 years.
* **Forecast**: future improvements are the curve of a posterior sample
  plus normal noise; values outside `limits` (0.005 and 0.035, as in the
  paper) are set to the nearest limit. Rates fall from the last smoothed
  rates by the forecast improvements (eq. 20 of the paper).
* **Uncertainty**: with `draws = "quantiles"` (the paper's method), draw
  `j` of `n` applies the quantile `(j - 0.5) / n` of the forecast
  improvements at every age and year, so the draws give the quantiles of
  the death rates of the paper. They are comonotone across ages and
  years; their order is permuted at random, so the draws of different
  strata are independent. `draws = "samples"` (package-specific) makes
  every draw one posterior predictive path, whose intervals of life
  expectancy are much narrower. Predictive draws add Poisson variation of
  the deaths given the rates.
* **Package-specific**: the origin of the time index, the floor of
  negative improvements in the least-squares values of the exponential
  model and the knots of the P-spline surface. The convergence of a
  population to the trend of reference populations is not implemented.
* **Use**: the paper recommends a base period at least as long as the
  forecast horizon, and single years of age from 0. In an example
  backtest on England & Wales men aged 30-100 (10 years ahead), the CRPS
  of log rates was 0.045 against 0.071 for Lee-Carter, and the 95%
  intervals covered 0.71 of the observed rates (Lee-Carter 0.63) and
  0.90 of the observed life expectancy at 30.

### Functional demographic model: `hyndman_ullah()`

Calls `demography::fdm()` (Hyndman and Ullah 2007): the rates of each
year are smoothed over age with `demography::smooth.demogdata()`
(`smooth = TRUE`; settings in `smooth_args`), and the log rates are
decomposed into a mean function and functional principal components,
whose scores are forecast with time-series models. The number of
components and the smoothing settings can be chosen by forecast accuracy
with `tuned()`. Draws are simulated
from the fitted model. Its intervals are those of the simulated paths,
which are somewhat narrower at short horizons than demography's analytic
intervals (see the comparison vignette). Predictive draws add Poisson
variation of the deaths given the rates. Without smoothing, the resampled
model errors already contain the observation noise, which predictive
draws then add a second time.

### Time series per age: `arima_series()`, `ets_series()`

Benchmarks that model the observed log rate of every age as a separate
time series with the forecast package (Hyndman and Khandakar 2008): an
ARIMA model chosen by `forecast::auto.arima()` (drift allowed) or given
by `order`, or an exponential smoothing model chosen by `forecast::ets()`
(damped trends allowed). `arima_series(order = c(0, 1, 1), drift = TRUE)`
is the local level model with drift (a random walk with drift observed
with noise; Harvey 1989) in its reduced form, fitted by maximum
likelihood: where deaths are few, it separates the noise of the observed
rates from the trend, which the plain random walk accumulates.
**Uncertainty**: simulated future paths of the fitted models, so the
intervals grow with the horizon; ages are simulated independently and
parameter uncertainty is not included. The series are observed rates, so
their draws already contain observation noise.

### StMoMo models: `stmomo()`

Calls `StMoMo::fit()` and `simulate()` (Villegas, Kaishev and
Millossovich 2018) for the Lee-Carter, CBD, APC, RH, M6, M7, M8 and Plat
families. M7 adds a quadratic age term and a cohort effect to CBD; M8 a
cohort effect that falls with age to zero at age `xc` (Cairns et al.
2009). `"rh"` is StMoMo's Renshaw-Haberman model with a cohort effect
without age modulation (`cohortAgeFun = "1"`, the default of StMoMo's
`rh()`). The period indexes follow a multivariate random walk with drift,
the cohort effects an ARIMA model (`gc_order`; by default ARIMA(2,0,0)
with a mean for M7 and the Plat model, as in the StMoMo vignette, and
ARIMA(1,1,0) with drift for the other models). For the models with a
logit link, initial exposures are central exposures plus half the deaths,
as `StMoMo::central2initial()`, and forecast probabilities of death are
converted to rates with `m = -log(1 - q)`. Draws contain the period and
cohort index uncertainty that StMoMo simulates; parameter uncertainty is
not included. Predictive draws add Poisson variation of the deaths given
the rates.

`stmomo("plat")` is the reduced Plat model for older ages as the StMoMo
vignette defines it: `logit q(x,t) = a(x) + k1(t) + (xbar - x) k2(t) +
g(t - x)`, with `xbar` the mean age of the data, built from the
vignette's age functions and constraints (both period indexes centred;
no level, linear or quadratic trend in the cohort effect, as in Haberman
and Renshaw 2011). Plat (2009) combines the CBD model with features of
the Lee-Carter model, uses the log link with Poisson deaths, and for all
ages adds a third period term, which he suggests dropping when only
older ages are of interest; the full model is not offered. The fitted
rates equal those of the vignette's code. In the vignette's 50-year
forecasts for England & Wales men aged 55-89 the rates of this model
increase, which the vignette calls implausible. In an example backtest
on the same men (1996-2001, 10 years ahead), its CRPS of log
rates was 0.071 against 0.073 for Lee-Carter, and its 95% intervals
covered 0.76 of the observed rates (Lee-Carter 0.62).

### Age-period-cohort-improvement model: `apci()` (opt-in)

`log m(x,t) = alpha(x) + beta(x) (t - tbar) + kappa(t) + gamma(t - x)`,
with `tbar` the mean year (Richards et al. 2019), on single years of age.

* **Estimation**: Poisson maximum likelihood with the five constraints of
  the paper's Appendix C. They are more than identification needs
  ("over-constrained", Section 6), as in the paper's main results.
  Cohorts with four or fewer cells get `gamma = 0` (Appendix B). With
  `smooth = TRUE` (the paper's APCI(S)), `alpha` and `beta` are P-splines
  with second-order penalties whose smoothing parameters minimise the BIC
  (Appendix D).
* **Forecast**: `beta(x) (t - tbar)` continues linearly. `kappa` and
  `gamma` follow ARIMA models without a mean, with orders chosen as in
  Appendix E: for `kappa` the best orders by AICc with one and with two
  differences, then the number of differences by the smaller RMSE (Solo
  1984); for `gamma` one difference and orders by AICc. `kappa_order` and
  `gamma_order` fix the orders.
* **Uncertainty**: innovations of `kappa` and `gamma`. The other
  parameters are fixed. Predictive draws add Poisson variation of the
  deaths given the rates.
* **Package-specific**: cubic B-splines with knots about five years apart
  (the paper gives no knots); the constraints enter as Lagrange conditions
  in penalised IRLS (the paper uses the augmented model matrix of Currie
  2013); the paper's value-at-risk framework is not implemented.
* **Use**: older ages with cohort effects. With two differences the
  forecasts of `kappa` can accelerate; fix `kappa_order` if that is not
  wanted. In an example backtest on England & Wales men aged 55-89
  (origins 1996-2001, 10 years ahead), the CRPS of log rates was 0.035
  against 0.072 for Lee-Carter, the 95% intervals covered 0.88 of the
  observed rates (Lee-Carter 0.63), and those of life expectancy at 55
  0.98.

### Bayesian StMoMo models: `stanmomo()`

The same families (Lee-Carter, RH, APC, CBD, M6) fitted with Stan by
StanMoMo (Barigou et al. 2023), with a Poisson or negative binomial
likelihood. Period indexes are random walks with drift (CBD and M6:
correlated), cohort effects AR(2) processes.

* **Forecast**: StanMoMo forecasts inside the fit, up to `h_max` years.
* **Uncertainty**: posterior draws of all parameters and of the future
  indexes. Predictive draws are draws of the posterior predictive
  distribution of the deaths: Poisson given the rates of each posterior
  draw, or, with `family = "nb"`, negative binomial with the dispersion of
  the same draw (Delwarde, Denuit and Partrat 2007).
* **Convergence**: the fit warns when the largest R-hat exceeds 1.05 or
  transitions diverged; models with cohort effects need longer chains.

### Bayesian age-period-cohort model: `apc_bayes()`

Calls `bamp::bamp()` (Schmid and Held 2007): logit death probability =
age + period + cohort effects with random-walk priors of order 1 or 2,
binomial likelihood, MCMC. Convergence is checked with the Gelman-Rubin
statistic of the identified quantities (reported by `mt_parameters()` as
`rhat`); chains that have not converged are refitted with longer runs.
**Uncertainty**: posterior samples of the forecast rates, including the
uncertainty of the parameters and of the random walks of period and cohort
effects; predictive draws add Poisson variation of the deaths given the
rates of each draw (bamp's binomial likelihood and overdispersion term
are not carried into them). Each stratum is fitted separately, by default
where the deaths were observed (5-year age groups with annual periods use
`periods_per_agegroup = 5`; Knorr-Held and Rainer 2001). `apc_select()`
compares random-walk orders by the deviance information criterion
(Spiegelhalter et al. 2002).

### Nordpred: `nordpred_apc()`

The Nordpred method of Møller et al. (2003) for projections of cancer
incidence and mortality: an age-period-cohort model of 5-year age groups
`a` and 5-year periods `p`, with Poisson deaths of mean
`E (A(a) + d p + P(p) + C(c))^5` (`link = "power5"`, default) or
`E exp(A(a) + d p + P(p) + C(c))` (`link = "log"`). The power 5 levels off
the exponential growth of the multiplicative model. The specification
follows the paper and the documentation of the R package nordpred 1.1;
the implementation is written independently, and its point projections
agree with those of nordpred to a relative difference below 1e-7.

* **Estimation**: Poisson generalised linear model with the power link.
  The prediction base is the largest candidate number of recent periods
  (`n_periods`, 4 to 6) whose fit the goodness-of-fit test does not
  reject at the 1% level, or the smallest if it rejects all. Age groups
  below `est_age` do not enter the regression.
* **Forecast**: the drift is projected; it is the slope of the last 10
  years when a quadratic period term is significant at the 5% level and
  the average drift otherwise (`recent = NULL`). It is cut by 0%, 25%,
  50%, 75% and 75% in the five future periods (`cut_trend`). Cohorts
  younger than that of age group `use_age` in the last period take its
  effect, and age groups below `use_age` keep the mean rate of the last
  two periods.
* **Package-specific**: annual data are summed to 5-year periods that end
  with the last training year, and annual rates are interpolated linearly
  in the linear predictor between the period midpoints. The age groups
  must be 5 years wide (`mt_regroup()`).
* **Uncertainty**: Nordpred gives point projections only. Each draw takes
  the coefficients from their asymptotic normal distribution
  (package-specific): the draws contain no variation of future period
  effects and no overdispersion. Predictive draws add Poisson variation
  of the deaths given the rates. In an example backtest on England &
  Wales men in 5-year groups from 30 (1996-2001, 10 years ahead), the 95%
  intervals covered 0.11 of the observed rates, and the CRPS of log rates
  was 0.079 against 0.069 for Lee-Carter on the same groups (0.066 with
  the log link). Use the projections as point forecasts, or widen the
  intervals with `recalibrated()`.

## Models for several populations

### Li-Lee: `li_lee()`

`log m(x,t,i) = a(x,i) + B(x) K(t) + b(x,i) k(t,i)` (Li and Lee 2005).

* **Estimation**: the common factor `B(x) K(t)` is a Lee-Carter model
  (SVD, `k` refitted to deaths) of the pooled deaths and exposures of the
  strata in a group (`common_by`, for example one common factor per sex);
  the stratum factors come from an SVD of the residual log rates.
* **Forecast**: `K(t)` random walk with drift; each `k(t,i)` an AR(1)
  process, so the deviations of a stratum from the common trend stay
  bounded ("coherent" in the sense that the strata do not diverge). Two
  choices of this package differ from Li and Lee (2005), whose AR(1)
  processes have a constant: the AR(1) processes have no intercept, so
  the stratum indexes revert to zero, and their coefficient is bounded to
  `|phi| <= 0.99` (a safeguard against unit roots, with a warning where
  the bound binds).
* **Jump-off**: fitted rates of the last year (default), or the forecasts
  multiplied by the ratio of observed to fitted rates of the last year
  (`jump_off = "observed"`; Lee and Miller 2001).
* **Uncertainty**: innovations and drift of `K(t)`, innovations of the
  AR(1) processes (independent across strata). `a`, `b`, `B` and `phi`
  are fixed. Predictive draws add Poisson variation of the deaths given
  the rates.

### Common age effect model: `cae()` (opt-in)

`log m(x,t,i) = a(x,i) + sum_j beta_j(x) kappa_j(t,i)`, with age effects
`beta_j` common to all populations and period effects of each population
(Kleinow 2015).

* **Estimation**: the log rates of each population are centred over the
  years (`a(x,i)` are their means). The common age effects are the common
  principal components of the populations, estimated by least squares
  with equal weight per population (Section 3.2; the paper modifies the
  maximum likelihood estimator of Flury 1984 so that large populations do
  not dominate). `kappa(t,i)` is the projection of the centred log rates
  on them. The columns of `beta` are orthonormal, and the period effects
  of each population sum to zero. `order` is the number of common age
  effects; the fit reports the mean squared error and the approximate BIC
  of eq. (4)-(5). As in the paper, the data need more years than age
  groups.
* **Forecast** (package-specific; the paper does not forecast): all
  period effects follow one multivariate random walk with drift with
  correlated innovations, as StMoMo forecasts several indexes. Each
  population keeps its own drift, so forecasts of different populations
  can diverge.
* **Uncertainty**: correlated innovations and the drift uncertainty;
  `a` and `beta` are fixed. Predictive draws add Poisson variation of the
  deaths given the rates.
* **Package-specific**: the paper's criterion is minimised by Jacobi
  rotations (Cardoso and Souloumiac 1996); the paper uses the F-G algorithm;
  the columns are ordered by the variation summed over populations; zero
  deaths are replaced by 0.5; `common_by` gives each group its own age
  effects, an extension the paper names; in a hierarchy the age effects
  come from the bottom strata.
* **Use**: populations that share the age pattern of change and differ in
  its speed. `vignette("dependence")` shows the dependence it gives to
  totals and gaps.

### Trend of a reference population and spreads: `saint()` (opt-in)

The SAINT model (Spread Adjusted InterNational Trend; Jarner and Kryger
2011) forecasts the adult mortality of small populations as stationary
deviations (spreads) from the trend of a large reference population.
mortensor implements the revised version of Jarner and Jallbjørn (2022),
which its authors describe as the model in use.

* **Trend**: the deaths and exposures of the reference strata (for example
  a national total or several countries) are pooled. Their rates follow a
  Gamma frailty model with a baseline that is log-linear in age with a
  kink at 75, and a background term (eqs. 5.1-5.3). For a given frailty
  variance the indexes of each year are the EM estimates of Appendix B;
  the variance maximises the profile pseudo-likelihood (eq. 4.14). `by`
  gives each group (for example each sex) its own trend. The level and
  slope of the baseline follow a random walk with drift, or with `ecm` an
  error-correction model that keeps the trends of two groups together
  (Section 5.2.1); the other indexes follow random walks without drift.
* **Spread**: the rates of each target stratum are the trend times
  `exp(y(t)' r(x))`, with five piecewise linear age regressors (eq. 5.11).
  `y(t)` is estimated year by year by Poisson maximum likelihood given the
  trend and follows a VAR(1) without mean (eq. 5.12), by default with a
  diagonal coefficient matrix with entries in `[0, 0.99]`, as the paper
  recommends. The spreads revert to zero, so the targets stay close to the
  trend.
* **Uncertainty**: innovations of the trend indexes and of the spreads;
  parameters are fixed, as in the papers. Predictive draws add Poisson
  variation of the deaths given the rates. Jump-off: fitted rates (Section
  5.3).
* **Ages**: consecutive single years from age 20 without an open interval;
  both papers use ages 20-100.
* **Package-specific** (listed on `?saint`): the EM fixed point computed by
  Newton-Raphson sweeps, the search of the frailty variance, the bounds of
  the spread coefficients, independent innovations of the indexes, three
  formulas of the 2022 paper read as misprints, and `background = FALSE`,
  a model of the class of Section 4.2 without the background term.
* **Use**: regions or small countries against a national or international
  reference. In an example on the German Laender against the national
  total (ages 20-89, 1998-2019, single ages by `mt_ungroup()`), the data
  did not identify the background of women (its estimate reached the
  lower bound from 2011 on), and 2.8% of the draws had rates above 1 at
  ages 20-23; warnings said so. With `background = FALSE` the forecasts
  were stable.

### Product-ratio: `coherent_fdm()`

The product-ratio method (Hyndman, Booth and Yasmeen 2013) models the
geometric mean of the strata (the product, which carries the common trend)
and the ratio of each stratum to it. `coherent_fdm()` is the original
method with the functional data models of demography:

* **Estimation**: the rates of each stratum are smoothed over age; the
  product and the ratios are decomposed into weighted principal components
  (`demography::fdm()`), with weights `beta (1 - beta)^i` for the year `i`
  years before the last and `beta = 0.05`, as in the applications of the
  paper (`weighted = FALSE` gives the unweighted default of
  `demography::coherentfdm()`). With `common_by`, each group has its own
  product; in a hierarchy only the bottom strata enter the product.
* **Forecast**: the scores of the product follow ARIMA models, those of the
  ratios stationary ARFIMA models, so the ratios return towards their
  recent level and the strata do not diverge. The fractional differencing
  parameter lies in `drange = c(0, 0.5)`, the default of demography (the
  paper names -0.5 < d < 0.5).
* **Uncertainty**: simulated scores and resampled model errors of the
  product and of each ratio (the paper gives analytic variances for the
  rates); the ratios of each path are rescaled to multiply to one, as
  `demography::forecast.fdmpr()` does for the point forecasts. Predictive
  draws add Poisson variation of the deaths given the rates.

`product_ratio()`, a Lee-Carter version of the method without a published
source, is deprecated in favour of `coherent_fdm()`.

### Multiway compositional model: `coda_multiway()` (experimental)

`coda_multiway()` is the three-way compositional model of
Bergeron-Boucher, Simonacci, Oeppen and Gallo (2018). The centred
log-ratios of the life-table deaths of all strata, each centred by its
geometric mean over the years, form an array `[age, year, stratum]`, and a
Tucker3 decomposition describes it:
`clr(d(x,t,i) / a(x,i)) = sum g(p,q,r) b(x,p) k(t,q) gamma(i,r)`, with age
patterns `b`, time indexes `k`, stratum markers `gamma` and a core array
`g`. With one component per mode (`ranks = c(1, 1, 1)`, the model of the
paper's forecasts), every stratum follows one time index and one age
pattern, at a pace set by its marker `gamma(i)`. With one stratum the fit
and the point forecasts are those of `coda()` with the same index model.

* **Estimation**: least squares by alternating least squares
  (higher-order orthogonal iteration); the paper uses the Tucker3 model
  for compositional data of Gallo (2015), which minimises the same
  criterion. `fit$fits$fit_pct` is the share of the variation that the
  model explains (Section 4.1 of the paper). The unit tests recover known
  parameters from simulated compositions and check the least-squares
  optimum.
* **Forecast**: the time index follows a random walk with drift, the
  ARIMA model that the paper selected for the index of Canadian women
  (`order`, `drift`). The paper states no jump-off adjustment, so
  forecasts start from the fitted deaths; `jump_off = "observed"` starts
  from the observed deaths as `coda()` does.
* **Uncertainty**: as in the paper, draws simulate the time index with
  resampled innovations; the other parameters and the drift are fixed,
  and all strata share the paths of the index. Predictive draws add
  Poisson variation of the deaths given the rates.
* **Choices where the paper is silent**: several time indexes get
  independent ARIMA models; old ages, open age intervals and zero deaths
  are treated as in `coda()`. The paper uses five-year age groups and
  periods; the models of this package need single calendar years. The
  choice of the ranks by the DifFit criterion, bootstrap confidence
  intervals of the parameters and the AIC comparison of the paper are not
  implemented.

The paper fits women and men separately (`stratified("sex", female =
coda_multiway(), male = coda_multiway())`). For populations whose age
and time patterns differ, the paper points to models with a common
component and deviations per population, such as `coda(coherent = TRUE)`
and `li_lee()` (its Section 6).

### Three-way Lee-Carter model: `tucker3()` (experimental)

`tucker3()` is the three-way extension of the Lee-Carter model of
Russolillo, Giordano and Haberman (2011). The mean log rate over the years
of each age and stratum is removed (eq. 7 of the paper), and the centred
array of log rates `[age, period, stratum]` is decomposed by a Tucker3
decomposition into column-wise orthonormal age, period and stratum factors
linked by a core array, estimated by least squares. Ranks `c(1, 1, 1)`
give one period index for all strata; the default `c(2, 2, 2)` is the
model of the paper's application to ten European countries.
`fit$fits$fit_pct` is the share of the variation of the centred array
that the model explains, the paper's measure of fit (its Table 4).

* **Estimation**: higher-order orthogonal iteration (De Lathauwer, De Moor
  and Vandewalle 2000). The paper uses Kiers' Tucker3 program for Matlab,
  another alternating least-squares algorithm for the same criterion.
  The paper's Matlab session also centres across ages; the package
  follows eq. (7).
* **Forecast**: the paper leaves the model of the period factors open.
  Here they follow a multivariate random walk with drift (`ts = "rwd"`),
  or ARIMA or ETS models per factor; this choice, the choice of the ranks
  by an information criterion (`ranks = "bic"` or `"aic"`) and 0.5 deaths
  in empty cells are package-specific.
* **Uncertainty**: draws resample the joint year-to-year changes of the
  period factors and include the uncertainty of the drift; the other
  factors and the core are fixed, and predictive draws add Poisson
  variation of the deaths given the rates. With fewer period factors than
  independent trends in the data, the strata share their forecast
  uncertainty and intervals are too narrow: on simulated Lee-Carter data
  with an own random walk in each of 10 strata, the 95% intervals covered
  about 74% with the default ranks and 95% with `ranks = c(1, 10, 10)`.
  `residual_noise = TRUE` adds the in-sample residual variation, which
  counts the observation noise twice.

`transform = "coda"` is deprecated (use `coda_multiway()`). The model is
experimental: compare it with established models such as `li_lee()` in a
backtest before using it.

### Causes of death

`coda_causes()` (experimental) is the multiple-decrement form of the
compositional model that Oeppen (2008) proposed and tested on Japanese
causes of death. In each group of strata (for example one per sex), the
deaths of a multiple-decrement life table by age and cause form one
composition, so the causes add up to all causes in every draw; cause
rates follow from the forecast deaths by the relations of the
multiple-decrement life table (eq. 7 of the paper).

* **Defaults**: one component and the index model of `coda()`. Oeppen
  (2008) used two components and ARIMA(0,2,2) models for Japanese women:
  `rank = 2, order = c(0, 2, 2)`. With several components, each index has
  its own ARIMA model.
* **Deviations**: Oeppen (2008) gives point forecasts only; the jump-off
  and the bootstrap draws are those of `coda()`. Zero counts are replaced
  multiplicatively (Oeppen smooths the deaths of each year lightly). The
  death rate of an open age interval is regressed on the indexes and
  split by cause through the composition, a residual cause covers deaths
  that the listed causes leave unexplained, and predictive draws split
  Poisson all-cause deaths multinomially between the causes, so that the
  causes add up in predictive draws as well (all package-specific).
* **Accuracy**: in an example backtest on simulated causes
  (`mt_example_causes()`, origins 2008-2012, 5 years ahead), its CRPS of
  log rates was 0.082, against 0.063 for Lee-Carter models per cause
  reconciled with WLS.

The alternative is separate models per cause made coherent with the
all-cause forecast by `reconciled()` (below). `cause_shares()`, a Tucker
model of cause shares without a published source, is deprecated.

## Jump-off: `anchored()`

Forecasts start from the fitted rates of the last year for most models.
`anchored()` moves the start of any model to the observed level: by
default the forecast draws are multiplied, per age and stratum, by the
ratio of observed to fitted deaths in the last training year, in every
forecast year. This is the jump-off adjustment of Lee and Miller (2001),
the same as `lee_carter(jump_off = "observed")`. Starting from the
observed rates of one year carries their random variation into every
forecast year, which matters where deaths are few. The other settings are
package-specific options: the offset of the last `years` years, shrunk
towards the stratum mean where deaths are few (`shrink = TRUE`, empirical
Bayes with the moment estimator of DerSimonian and Laird 1986), and a
linear fade over `decay` years. `mt_jump_off()` reports the step between
the last observed (and fitted) year and the first forecast year.

## Combining models

### Ensembles: `ensemble()`

A mixture (linear pool; Gneiting and Ranjan 2013) of the predictive
distributions of its components: each draw comes from one component, for
all strata at once, chosen with probabilities equal to the weights. The
weights are equal by default. The other weights come from an inner
rolling-origin backtest on the training years, so they use no data after
the forecast origin:

* `weights = "crps_stack"` is stacking of predictive distributions (Yao
  et al. 2018, Section 2.1, eq. 2.2): the weights on the simplex that
  minimise the mean CRPS of the mixture over the inner forecasts of the
  log rates. Yao et al. allow any proper scoring rule and use the
  logarithmic score; the CRPS (Gneiting and Raftery 2007), computed from
  the draws, is the choice of this package. The mean CRPS of the mixture
  is a convex quadratic function of the weights (kernel form of the CRPS,
  Gneiting and Raftery 2007, eq. 21), minimised exactly.
* `weights = "bias"` follows Kontis et al. (2017): each component is
  fitted without the last 13 training years, its projection bias is the
  observed minus the projected life expectancy averaged over these years,
  and its weight is `exp(-|bias|)`. The life expectancy is that at the
  first age of the data; with several strata, one weight per component
  comes from the mean absolute bias over the strata (package-specific;
  the paper weights each population separately, which `stratified()`
  does).
* `weights = "crps"` takes weights inverse to the mean CRPS of each
  component. Shang (2012) weights point forecasts inverse to their mean
  absolute errors, following Bates and Granger (1969); the CRPS of a
  point forecast is its absolute error, and the extension to predictive
  distributions is package-specific.
* `weights = "stack"` is deprecated: it stacks the median forecasts
  (Breiman 1996; for mortality, Kessy et al. 2022) and uses the weights,
  which optimise the weighted mean of the medians, as mixture
  probabilities.

`top_k` keeps the components with the lowest inner CRPS
(package-specific). The mixture contains the uncertainty of each
component and the disagreement between them.

### Different models for groups of strata: `stratified()`

One model per level of a stratum variable, for example Lee-Carter for
all-cause mortality and Li-Lee for the causes of death. The groups are
fitted and forecast separately and their draws combined; inside
`reconciled()` they can be made coherent, for example with the causes
scaled to the all-cause forecast.

### Reconciled forecasts: `reconciled()`

Forecasts of all nodes of a hierarchy (bottom strata and their totals)
are made to add up draw by draw: bottom-up sums, or projections of the
base forecasts with weights from their variances (WLS; Hyndman, Lee and
Wang 2016), the shrunk covariance (MinT; Wickramasuriya, Athanasopoulos
and Hyndman 2019, with the shrinkage of Schäfer and Strimmer 2005), the
structure (structural scaling; Athanasopoulos et al. 2017) or equal
weights (OLS; Hyndman et al. 2011). The variances and covariances of WLS
and MinT are those of the base forecast draws in each age and forecast
year; the papers use the in-sample residuals of the base models.

Where a projection makes bottom values of a draw negative, that draw is
reconciled by the non-negative reconciliation of Wickramasuriya, Turlach
and Hyndman (2020): the bottom values minimise the same weighted distance
subject to being non-negative, a quadratic program solved by their block
principal pivoting algorithm, and the aggregates are their sums. A
warning reports when more than 5% of the draws have bottom values at
zero, because the distributions of those strata are then truncated.
`fixed` nodes (a trusted total) are kept, as in the reconciliation with
immutable forecasts of Zhang et al. (2023): they get a near-zero variance
(1e-10 of the largest), and with MinT the other nodes get their
covariance conditional on the fixed nodes, so that the fixed nodes are
equality constraints of the weighted least-squares problem, also in the
non-negative quadratic program. With fixed nodes, `"proportional"` scales
their parts in proportion to their forecasts (top-down allocation; Gross
and Sohl 1990; Athanasopoulos, Ahmed and Hyndman 2009). Deaths add up
over every hierarchy variable; exposures add up over variables that
divide the population and are shared by the levels of variables such as
causes of death (`additive = "rates"`). The exposures of the forecast
years are those of the last observed year unless projections are given.
The draws are reconciled as they are (`dependence = "none"`, default);
`dependence = "empirical"` reorders the paths of separately fitted strata
first, a package-specific method related to the Schaake shuffle (Clark et
al. 2004).

Score-optimal reconciliation (`method = "energy_score"`; Panagiotelis et
al. 2023) learns the reconciliation from the base model's own past
forecasts: the reconciled draws are `S (d + G y)`, where `y` are the base
draws of all nodes, and the free parameters `d` and `G` minimise the total
energy score of forecasts from `n_origins` inner origins in the last
`years` of the training data, by stochastic gradient descent (Adam with
the settings of the paper) from OLS, as in the package ProbReco. Details
of this package: one `d` and `G` per age; inner models on expanding
windows; horizons 1 to `horizon` in one objective (the paper: one
horizon); observation noise in the training forecasts; 50 draws per
step taken from a fixed set of inner draws (the paper: 250, simulated
afresh); a rescaling of the nodes before the optimisation; and bottom
values below zero set to zero in the forecast. It has many parameters and
few training forecasts; in the package's backtests it was less accurate
than WLS.

### Dependence from a joint model: `coupled()` (opt-in)

Separate models per stratum give forecasts whose errors are independent
across strata. `coupled(spec, template)` keeps the forecast distribution
of `spec` in every cell and takes the dependence between cells from a
template, usually a joint model such as `li_lee()` or `cae()`. The method
is ensemble copula coupling (Schefzik, Thorarinsdottir and Gneiting
2013): in each cell (age, year, stratum) the draws of `spec` are sorted
and assigned in the rank order of the template's draws. This is the
paper's ECC-R variant, for draws that are a random sample of each margin;
tied template values are ranked at random (footnote 6). Every cell keeps
its values exactly, and the rank correlations between cells are those of
the template. `mt_couple()` couples two sets of forecast draws, and
`reconciled(..., dependence = "ecc", template = )` couples before
reconciliation. Package-specific: the coupling acts on the draws of the
rates before observation noise, which predictive draws add afterwards.
`vignette("dependence")` explains why the dependence matters for totals,
gaps and inequality measures.

### Calibration on recent years: `recalibrated()`

Refits a model at several origins in the last `years` (default 10) of
the training data, compares its forecasts with the observed rates of that
window, and rescales the spread of the draws around their median per cell
by one factor for all horizons that minimises the CRPS (or the interval
score of one interval), with the Poisson variation of the observed deaths
(negative binomial for `stanmomo(family = "nb")`) as in a backtest. The
closest published method is the member-by-member post-processing of
ensemble forecasts (Van Schaeybroeck and Vannitsem 2015); the
minimum-CRPS estimation follows Gneiting et al. (2005). Ranks within each
cell are kept, so the draws remain paths. Calibration widens models that
were persistently too narrow (Lee-Carter on England & Wales men: 95%
coverage 0.63 to 0.85 in the backtest of "Tuning and recalibration") and
can narrow mixtures that were already wide. Package-specific options: a
factor that changes with the horizon as `s1 h^gamma` (`scale =
"horizon"`), a correction of the drift (`bias = TRUE`), separate factors
for age bands (`ages`) and calibration of the intervals of life
expectancy or the ASR (`quantity`), which also depend on how the ages move
together; `n_boot` reports bootstrap intervals of the factors. Beyond the
longest horizon of the window the factors stay constant. Calibration
keeps the model and its settings; choosing the settings themselves is
tuning (below).

### Bootstrap and tuning: `bootstrapped()`, `tuned()`

`bootstrapped()` refits a model to Poisson resamples of the deaths
(parameter uncertainty): of the fitted deaths on the grid (`type =
"grid"`, default; Renshaw and Haberman 2008), or of the observed deaths at
their original resolution with the preprocessing refitted as well (`type =
"data"`; Brouhns, Denuit and Van Keilegom 2005; refitting the
preprocessing is an extension of this package).
`tuned()` chooses settings by how well they forecast the last years of
the training data only (rolling-origin evaluation, Tashman 2000;
`mt_tune()` shows the scores): model settings
such as the number of components or the rank, and with `spec_fun`
returning `list(spec = , prep = )` preprocessing settings such as the
smoothing parameter or the fitting window. `inner_origins = 1, inner_h =
10` is the hold-out of the last ten years often used with
`demography::fdm()`; several origins make the choice depend less on one
period. The criterion can be the CRPS, the interval score or point
accuracy (`metric = "rmse"`) of rates, life expectancy or ASR (`target`);
`select = "one_se"` takes the simplest setting within one standard error
of the best (Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman 2009), and `by` tunes groups
of strata separately. The fitting period matters for Lee-Carter forecasts
when the pace of decline changed (Booth, Maindonald and Smith 2002);
`step_window(years)` makes it a preprocessing step that tuning compares
across windows.

## Sources of uncertainty at a glance

| Model | Index innovations | Drift | Parameters | Observation noise |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `lee_carter()` | yes | yes | with `bootstrap = TRUE` | Poisson, predictive draws (negative binomial with `family = "nb"`) |
| `rwd()` | yes (observed changes) | yes | no | contained in the changes |
| `p_splines()` | no index; the penalty extends the coefficients, with variance growing with the horizon | in the coefficients | yes (normal approximation of the coefficients) | Poisson, predictive draws |
| `cp_splines()` | no | through the bootstrap | yes (residual bootstrap of the fit) | Poisson, predictive draws |
| `bohk_rau()` | yes (noise of the future improvements) | posterior (curve of each age) | yes (posterior) | Poisson, predictive draws |
| `arima_series()`, `ets_series()` | yes | as the fitted model | no | contained in the series |
| `li_lee()` | yes (common and stratum) | common factor | no | Poisson, predictive draws |
| `cae()` | yes (correlated across populations) | yes | no | Poisson, predictive draws |
| `saint()` | yes (trend indexes and spreads) | level and slope of the trend | no | Poisson, predictive draws |
| `coherent_fdm()` | yes (product and ratios) | as fdm (product) | no | Poisson, predictive draws |
| `tucker3()` | yes (period factors) | yes | no | Poisson, predictive draws (with `residual_noise = TRUE` also the residual variation) |
| `coda()`, `coda_causes()` | yes (resampled innovations) | yes (index model refitted) | `b`, `k` and the index model (residual bootstrap); `a` fixed | Poisson, predictive draws (`coda_causes()`: all-cause deaths split multinomially between the causes) |
| `coda_multiway()` | yes (resampled innovations, shared by the strata) | no | no | Poisson, predictive draws |
| `hyndman_ullah()` | yes | as fdm | no | Poisson, predictive draws |
| `stmomo()` (including `"plat"`) | yes | yes | no | Poisson, predictive draws |
| `apci()` | yes (`kappa` and `gamma`) | the linear term continues | no | Poisson, predictive draws |
| `stanmomo()` | yes | posterior | yes (posterior) | Poisson or negative binomial (posterior predictive), predictive draws |
| `apc_bayes()` | yes | posterior | yes (posterior) | Poisson, predictive draws |
| `nordpred_apc()` | no (no variation of future period effects) | yes (a coefficient) | yes (asymptotic normal distribution of the coefficients) | Poisson, predictive draws |
| `ensemble()` | of the components | of the components | of the components, plus model choice | of the components |
| `stratified()` | of the model of each group | of the model of each group | of the model of each group | as the models |
| `bootstrapped()` | of the base model | of the base model | yes | as the base model |
| `reconciled()` | of the base model, projected | | | of the bottom strata, summed |
| `coupled()` | of the base model, reordered | of the base model | of the base model | as the base model |
| `recalibrated()` | of the base model, rescaled | rescaled (optional correction) | | as the base model |
| `anchored()` | of the base model | of the base model | | as the base model |

The deprecated `rwd(observation_noise = TRUE)`, `product_ratio()` and
`cause_shares()` are left out.

Predictive draws (`predictive = TRUE`, always used in backtests) describe
observable rates. For models of expected rates they are deaths drawn
given the rates of each draw and the exposures, divided by the exposures:
Poisson, the observation model of the Poisson Lee-Carter model (Brouhns,
Denuit and Vermunt 2002), or negative binomial with the estimated
dispersion for `lee_carter(family = "nb")` and with the dispersion of the
posterior draw for `stanmomo(family = "nb")`. No other observation noise
is added. For models of observed rates (`rwd()`, `arima_series()`,
`ets_series()`) the draws already describe observable rates and nothing
is added, unless the model was fitted to smoothed rates (`step_smooth()`):
then predictive draws add Poisson deaths as well. Forecast draws of
models of expected rates without `predictive` describe the expected
rates. If intervals are too narrow on real data, that is a property of
the model; `recalibrated()`, `ensemble()` and overdispersed models such
as `lee_carter(family = "nb")` and `stanmomo(family = "nb")` widen them.

## Evaluation

`mt_backtest()` refits preprocessing and model at each origin and scores
predictive draws against the observed log rates of the test years with the
continuous ranked probability score (CRPS; Gneiting and Raftery 2007), the
weighted interval score (Bracher et al. 2021), interval coverage, the
probability integral transform and the absolute error of the median. Cells
with estimated (suppressed) deaths are not scored unless
`score_estimated = TRUE`. `mt_dm_test()` tests differences in accuracy
between two models of the same backtest with the Diebold-Mariano test
(Diebold and Mariano 1995): by default with the equal-weighted cosine
estimate of the long-run variance and fixed-smoothing critical values
from a t distribution (Lazarus et al. 2018), whose size is nearly correct
with few overlapping origins, at the cost of low power.
`varestimator = "daniell"` gives the fixed-smoothing test of Coroneo and
Iacone (2020) with a Daniell-kernel estimate, which has more degrees of
freedom; with 7 overlapping origins its size was close to 5% up to
`h = 2` and too large beyond (15% at `h = 5`). `varestimator = "acf"`
gives the version of `forecast::dm.test()` with the correction of Harvey,
Leybourne and Newbold (1997), which rejects a true null hypothesis too
often with few overlapping origins.
